title: 09 — Bitemporal Modelling
html:
09 — Bitemporal Modelling

The one idea: store two independent timelines for every fact — valid time (when it was true in the world) and knowledge time (when you recorded that belief) — and never overwrite. Then any question of the form "what did we believe, on date K, about date V?" is a simple filter, and every past report can be reproduced exactly.

1. The problem

A company reports FY2024-25 revenue of 1,000 in May 2025. In June your team notices a parsing error: it was 1,010. In May 2026 the company restates FY2024-25 to 980 because a business was discontinued.

Three questions, three different correct answers:

Question Answer
What is FY24-25 revenue now? 980
What did our model use when it ran on 31 May 2025? 1,000
What was the best-known figure on 31 December 2025? 1,010

A table that keeps only the latest value can answer the first. Iceberg time travel can partly answer the second (if snapshots were not expired). Only a bitemporal table answers all three by design, forever, with SQL.

2. Definitions

Term Meaning Columns
Valid time (business / effective time) The period during which the fact is true in the real world valid_from, valid_to
Knowledge time (transaction / system / record time) The period during which the platform held this version as its belief known_from, known_to
Uni-temporal Only one of the two (e.g. SCD type 2 tracks one) —
Bitemporal Both, independently All four ("4-clock")

All intervals are half-open: [from, to). "Open-ended" is 9999-12-31.

3. Three kinds of change — keep them distinct

Change type What happened Valid period Example
Update The world changed A new valid period starts NAV for a new day; a new rating takes effect
Correction We recorded it wrong Same valid period, new knowledge version Parser read 1,000 instead of 1,010
Restatement The source revised its own published figure Same valid period, new knowledge version, new source document Company restates prior-year revenue in a later annual report

Each new version carries source, reason and approver. Corrections and restatements look the same structurally but mean different things: one is your error, the other is the issuer's revision. Analysts need to tell them apart (restatement frequency is itself a risk signal).

4. Table design

4.1 Append-only event table (recommended on a lakehouse)

Store only known_from; derive known_to with a window function. Rows are never updated, which fits immutable Parquet files and Iceberg appends perfectly.

CREATE TABLE silver.financial_fact_event (
  entity_id     STRING      NOT NULL,     -- canonical entity ID (chapter 10)
  metric        STRING      NOT NULL,     -- 'revenue', 'total_assets', …
  valid_from    DATE        NOT NULL,
  valid_to      DATE        NOT NULL,
  value         DECIMAL(18,2),
  unit          STRING      NOT NULL,     -- 'INR_CRORE'
  known_from    TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,     -- when this version entered the platform (or was published)
  change_type   STRING      NOT NULL,     -- INITIAL | UPDATE | CORRECTION | RESTATEMENT
  source_ref    STRING      NOT NULL,     -- file hash + page + bounding box
  reason        STRING,
  approved_by   STRING      NOT NULL,
  version_id    STRING      NOT NULL      -- unique per row
)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (metric, years(valid_from));

CREATE VIEW silver.financial_fact AS
SELECT *,
       coalesce(lead(known_from) OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id, metric, valid_from ORDER BY known_from),
                TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00') AS known_to
FROM silver.financial_fact_event;

4.2 Physically closed rows (classic design)

Store all four columns and update known_to of the superseded row in the same transaction as inserting the new one. Faster to query (no window), but it is an update — on Iceberg that is a MERGE that rewrites or deletes rows. Use it for current-state serving tables; keep the event table as the source of truth.

4.3 Which knowledge time?

Decide explicitly and document it in the contract:

  • Platform knowledge time — when you loaded it (reproduces what your systems saw).
  • Publication time — when the source published it (reproduces what the market could have known; avoids look-ahead bias in back-tests).

Many teams store both: known_from (platform) and published_at (source).

5. Querying — the four standard questions

Verified with DuckDB on the example in section 1:

-- 1. Current view: latest belief about every period
SELECT entity_id, metric, valid_from, value
FROM silver.financial_fact
WHERE known_to = TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00';

-- 2. As-of knowledge: what did we believe at K about every period?
SELECT valid_from, value, change_type
FROM silver.financial_fact
WHERE TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31 00:00:00' >= known_from
  AND TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31 00:00:00' <  known_to;
-- FY24-25 -> 1010 (CORRECTION)

-- 3. Fully bitemporal point: value valid at V as known at K
SELECT value
FROM silver.financial_fact
WHERE entity_id = 'E1' AND metric = 'revenue'
  AND DATE '2024-12-31' >= valid_from AND DATE '2024-12-31' < valid_to
  AND TIMESTAMP '2025-05-31 00:00:00' >= known_from
  AND TIMESTAMP '2025-05-31 00:00:00' <  known_to;
-- -> 1000 (INITIAL);  with K = 2026-10-31 -> 980 (RESTATEMENT);  with K = 2025-01-01 -> no row (not yet known)

-- 4. Audit trail: every version of one fact
SELECT known_from, known_to, value, change_type, reason, approved_by, source_ref
FROM silver.financial_fact
WHERE entity_id = 'E1' AND metric = 'revenue' AND valid_from = DATE '2024-04-01'
ORDER BY known_from;

5.1 Restatement analytics

-- How much did each restatement move the number, and how often does each entity restate?
-- Compute the previous version over ALL versions first, then keep only the restatements
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT entity_id, metric, valid_from, known_from, change_type,
         value - lag(value) OVER w                 AS change,
         (value / lag(value) OVER w - 1) * 100     AS change_pct
  FROM silver.financial_fact
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY entity_id, metric, valid_from ORDER BY known_from)
)
WHERE change_type = 'RESTATEMENT';

6. Writing — step by step

  1. A validated batch arrives from the quality gate (chapter 08).
  2. For each incoming fact, look up the current version for (entity_id, metric, valid_from).
  3. Classify:
    • no current version → INITIAL (or UPDATE if it starts a new valid period),
    • same value → skip (idempotent re-delivery),
    • different value, same source document → CORRECTION (needs reason + approver),
    • different value, newer source document → RESTATEMENT.
  4. Append the new versions in one commit.
import polars as pl

def classify(incoming: pl.DataFrame, current: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    key = ["entity_id", "metric", "valid_from"]
    j = incoming.join(current.select(*key, pl.col("value").alias("cur_value"),
                                     pl.col("source_doc").alias("cur_doc")),
                      on=key, how="left")
    return (
        j.with_columns(
            change_type=pl.when(pl.col("cur_value").is_null()).then(pl.lit("INITIAL"))
                          .when(pl.col("value") == pl.col("cur_value")).then(pl.lit("NOCHANGE"))
                          .when(pl.col("source_doc") == pl.col("cur_doc")).then(pl.lit("CORRECTION"))
                          .otherwise(pl.lit("RESTATEMENT"))
        )
        .filter(pl.col("change_type") != "NOCHANGE")
        .drop("cur_value", "cur_doc")
    )

7. Bitemporal + Iceberg — how they fit

Mechanism Answers Lifetime
Iceberg snapshots / time travel "What did the table contain at commit X?" (system time, physical) Until snapshots expire
Iceberg tags (vintage_YYYY_MM_DD) "Exactly which data did the certified release use?" As long as tag retention
Bitemporal columns "What did we believe about period V at time K?" (business logic) Forever, in the data itself

Use all three: bitemporal columns for business history, tags to pin certified releases, snapshots for operational rollback.

8. Common mistakes

  • Using closed intervals (BETWEEN) — creates overlaps at boundaries.
  • Storing known_to as NULL and forgetting IS NULL in some queries — use a sentinel or handle explicitly everywhere.
  • Treating a restatement as a correction (loses the risk signal) or as an update (creates a wrong new valid period).
  • Back-testing with platform knowledge time when you meant publication time → look-ahead bias.
  • Expiring Iceberg snapshots and assuming history is gone — it is not, if the table is bitemporal.

9. Questions to test yourself

  1. Explain the difference between an update, a correction and a restatement with one NAV example each.
  2. Write the query: "the rating of every issuer as it was in force on 31 March 2026, as known on 15 April 2026".
  3. Why does an append-only event table suit Parquet and Iceberg better than closing rows in place?
  4. Which knowledge time should a credit model back-test use, and why?
  5. How do bitemporal columns and Iceberg tags complement each other?

10. Review checklist

  • Every Silver fact table has valid_from, valid_to, known_from (and derived known_to).
  • Half-open intervals; open end is a sentinel date.
  • Change type, source reference, reason and approver on every version.
  • No in-place overwrites in the event table.
  • The contract states which knowledge time is used.
